link.note: Probable, strong (about 85–90%): her father's 1662 will names 'daughter Sarah Smith' and 'Adam Smith, son of daughter, Sarah', and the 1640 Winthrop letters describe 'Mr. Smith' contracted to 'my brother Hammond's daughter' at Watertown. No record names her husband as Richard; on John's side the whole line also rests on Keturah Tuttle's parentage.

death.place: Smithtown, Suffolk County, New York, USA

summary: Wife of Bull Smith, who sailed from Ipswich to New England in 1634 at the age of ten; John's 10th-great-grandmother.
bio:
Sarah Hammond was born about 1623 at Lavenham in Suffolk, a daughter of William Hammond. She was probably the 'Marie, daughter of William Hamond' whose baptism the Lavenham register records on 21 October, under a year that reads 1628 but is probably a misprint for 1623; the identification of Marie with Sarah is speculative. In April 1634, aged ten, she sailed from Ipswich on the Francis with her mother, 47, her sister Elizabeth, 15, and her brother John, 7, to join her father in New England.

Her engagement in 1640 left a mark in the governor's own papers. That April the Watertown minister, the Rev. George Phillips, and her uncle William Paine both wrote to Governor John Winthrop about a quarrel between "Mr. Smith" and "my brother Hammond's daughter". Smith and the young woman had promised to marry, the promise had been "publikely sett vpon our meeting house", and Smith was now trying to back out; he was "in the Bay" only for the moment, a man from outside Massachusetts. Before Winthrop and the Treasurer he admitted that he and her father had agreed on her marriage portion. Sarah was sixteen and her sisters were already married, so the "yong mayd" can only have been her, and the match went ahead: she became the wife of Richard Smith, later the patentee of Smithtown, known as Bull Smith. When her father made his will in 1662 he remembered "daughter Sarah Smith" and "Adam Smith, son of daughter, Sarah", and Bull Smith and Sarah had a son Adam, born in 1649; no other Adam Smith is known in New England before 1692. Pelletreau's history of 1898 called her "Sarah Folger, of Boston, according to all accounts", a tradition with no record behind it, and the 1902 Hammond genealogy's statement that she "separated" from her husband misread the 1640 dispute over the engagement as a failed marriage. In 1688 she joined her husband as a party to deeds made 'by and with the consent of Sarah his wife', acknowledging them with him on 17 September 1688.

Her will of 1707/8 left 'my son Richard's eldest sonne my blunderbuss', the gun known as 'Old Crib', which family tradition says the Patentee's father had carried in Cromwell's wars; in 1898 it was held by the heirs of Judge J. Lawrence Smith. The will also left a cow to Mr. George Phillips, the minister at Setauket, who bore the name of the Watertown pastor of her girlhood, and made her son Richard give up debts he 'pretends' were owed to him. She died at Smithtown in 1708.
funFacts: Owned the blunderbuss 'Old Crib', a family heirloom still held by descendants in 1898.

Winthrop Papers letters of 21 and 24 Apr 1640 (William Paine; Rev. George Phillips) found: the contested engagement of 'Mr. Smith' and Hammond's daughter, promise posted on the meeting house, portion agreed with her father. Savage: no Adam Smith in New England before 1692. Corrects the 1902 'separated' reading. Still missing: a record naming her husband as Richard.

researchNotes:
Sailed from Ipswich on the Francis in April 1634, aged 10, with her mother (47), Elizabeth (15) and John (7) (Hammond 1902). No Lavenham baptism under 'Sarah' found; Hammond's register list has 'Marie, daughter of William Hamond' dated 21 Oct '1628', probably a misprint for 1623 (it sits before the 1626 entry); WikiTree Hammond-356 suggests she was christened 'Marie' 21 Oct 1623 (speculative). Married Richard Smith in 1640 despite his attempt to withdraw. Her will of 1707/8 left 'my son Richard's eldest sonne my blunderbuss' — 'Old Crib', which family tradition says the Patentee's father used in Cromwell's wars; in 1898 it was held by the heirs of Judge J. Lawrence Smith. The will also left Mr. George Phillips a cow and made son Richard give up debts he 'pretends' were owed him (Pelletreau pp. 37–38). Pelletreau (1898) had called her 'Sarah Folger, of Boston, according to all accounts' — superseded.

Pelletreau prints the 1688 deeds that Sarah Smith joined as party ('by and with the consent of Sarah his wife'), acknowledged with her husband on 17 Sept 1688 ([R4-S1]). Her maiden name and Lavenham baptism were not re-examined this round.
